title: Spectral Terms in Atomic Physics
short_intro: Spectral terms denote the energy states of multi-electron atoms characterized by total orbital, spin, and total angular momentum quantum numbers. They provide a concise nomenclature for classifying atomic energy levels and optical transitions.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of term symbols for single-valence electron systems (like alkali atoms), quantum numbers n, l, s, j, and simple transitions using selection rules.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced coupling schemes (L-S and j-j coupling), Hund's rules for ground state determination, Landé interval rule, and Zeeman effect considerations.

prerequisites: Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom and quantum numbers
Pauli's exclusion principle and orbital degeneracy

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Anatomy of a Spectral Term
bullets: A spectral term is represented in the spectroscopic notation as <sup>2S+1</sup>L<sub>J</sub>, where S is the total spin quantum number, L is the total orbital angular momentum quantum number represented by letters (S, P, D, F, G...), and J is the total electronic angular momentum quantum number.
The multiplicity of the term is given by (2S+1), which indicates the number of sublevels associated with spin-orbit coupling for a given L and S (when L ≥ S).
The quantum number J takes values ranging from |L-S| to L+S in integer steps, representing vector addition of total orbital and spin angular momenta.

concept_notes.heading: L-S Coupling (Russell-Saunders Coupling)
bullets: Applicable predominantly to light and medium-mass atoms where electrostatic Coulomb interactions and exchange energies are much stronger than spin-orbit interactions.

Individual orbital angular momenta (l<sub>i</sub>) couple to form a resultant total orbital angular momentum L = ∑ l<sub>i</sub>, and individual spin angular momenta (s<sub>i</sub>) couple to form a resultant total spin S = ∑ s<sub>i</sub>.
L and S then couple weakly via spin-orbit interaction to form the total angular momentum J = L + S.

concept_notes.heading: j-j Coupling
bullets: Applicable to heavy multi-electron atoms where the spin-orbit interaction of individual electrons exceeds the electrostatic interaction between different electrons.
Each electron's orbital angular momentum l<sub>i</sub> couples strongly with its own spin s<sub>i</sub> to form an individual total angular momentum j<sub>i</sub> = l<sub>i</sub> + s<sub>i</sub>.
The individual j<sub>i</sub> vectors then couple weakly to yield the total electronic angular momentum J = ∑ j<sub>i</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Hund's Rules for Ground State Determination
bullets: Rule 1: For a given electron configuration, the term with the maximum multiplicity (2S+1) lies lowest in energy due to minimization of electrostatic repulsion (Pauli exclusion principle keeps parallel-spin electrons apart).
Rule 2: For terms with the same multiplicity, the term with the largest value of total orbital angular momentum L lies lowest in energy.

Rule 3: For outer shells less than half-filled, the level with the lowest J value (J = |L-S|) has the lowest energy (normal multiplet). For shells more than half-filled, the level with the highest J value (J = L+S) has the lowest energy (inverted multiplet).

derivations.title: Derivation of Total Angular Momentum J Range in L-S Coupling
derivations.conditions: Vector addition model of angular momenta in quantum mechanics
steps: Write the operators for total orbital angular momentum L and total spin S.
Apply quantum mechanical vector addition rules for angular momenta: |L - S| ≤ J ≤ L + S.
Determine the allowed integer steps for J based on the triangle inequality and spatial quantization of angular momentum.

derivations.title: Calculation of Multiplicity and Number of Components
derivations.conditions: L ≥ S condition for Russell-Saunders coupling
steps: Identify the number of unpaired electrons n in the subshell.
Determine the multiplicity as (2S+1) and count the distinct J values from |L-S| to L+S.
derivations.result: Number of J components equals 2S+1 when L ≥ S, and 2L+1 when L < S.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Vector Model of L-S Coupling
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Vectors L and S precessing rapidly about their resultant J vector, which in turn precesses slowly about the external magnetic field axis Z.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the quantum mechanical addition of angular momenta and the relative orientation of magnetic moments.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions regarding spatial quantization and precession.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Multiplet Splitting (Normal vs Inverted)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Energy level diagrams showing level spacing for J values where lower J is lower in energy (less than half-filled shell) versus higher J being lower in energy (more than half-filled shell).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes Hund's third rule and the effect of spin-orbit interaction on fine structure.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT exams for identifying ground state term configurations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Zeeman Splitting of Spectral Terms
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Splitting of a single <sup>3</sup>P<sub>1</sub> term into (2J+1) equidistant sublevels (m<sub>J</sub> = -1, 0, 1) under an applied magnetic field.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the lifting of spatial degeneracy of spectral terms in a magnetic field.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core concept for normal and anomalous Zeeman effect problems.

solved_numericals.question: Find the spectroscopic term symbol for an electron configuration with L = 1 and S = 1/2.
solution_steps: Identify the letter for L = 1, which is P.
Determine possible J values: J = L + S to |L - S| = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2 and 1 - 1/2 = 1/2.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the ground state spectral term for carbon atom (atomic number Z = 6) using Hund's rules.
solution_steps: Write the electronic configuration of carbon: 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>2</sup>.
Consider the valence electrons in the 2p subshell (n=2, l=1). The magnetic quantum numbers m<sub>l</sub> are +1, 0, -1.
To maximize multiplicity (Hund's Rule 1), place two electrons in separate orbitals with parallel spins: m<sub>l1</sub> = +1 (s=+1/2) and m<sub>l2</sub> = 0 (s=+1/2).
Total orbital angular momentum L = ∑ m<sub>l</sub> = +1 + 0 = +1, which corresponds to P.
Since the 2p shell is less than half-filled (2 electrons out of 6), apply Hund's Rule 3: J = |L - S| = |1 - 1| = 0.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the Landé g-factor for the spectral term <sup>2</sup>D<sub>3/2</sub>.
solution_steps: Identify the quantum numbers from <sup>2</sup>D<sub>3/2</sub>: Multiplicity 2S+1 = 2 ⇒ S = 1/2. Letter D ⇒ L = 2. J = 3/2.
Substitute values into the Landé g-factor formula: g = 1 + [J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)] / [2J(J+1)].

assumptions_and_limitations: Russell-Saunders coupling assumes electrostatic forces dominate over magnetic spin-orbit interactions, which breaks down for heavy atoms where j-j coupling must be used.
Central field approximation assumes each electron moves in an average spherically symmetric potential created by the nucleus and other electrons.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The multiplicity (2S+1) always represents the number of sub-levels in a fine structure multiplet.
common_misconceptions.correct: The number of fine structure levels is (2S+1) only when L ≥ S. If L < S, the number of levels is (2L+1).
common_misconceptions.why: J values are constrained by vector triangle inequalities |L-S| to L+S.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Hund's third rule always gives lowest energy for J = L - S.
common_misconceptions.correct: J = L - S is lowest only for subshells less than half-filled; for more than half-filled shells, J = L + S is lowest.
common_misconceptions.why: Spin-orbit coupling sign inverts due to negative effective nuclear charge gradient or orbital-spin orientation changes in fuller subshells.

quick_revision: L values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 correspond to S, P, D, F, G letters.
Hund's 2nd rule: Maximize L for same multiplicity.
Hund's 3rd rule: J = |L-S| for < half-filled, J = L+S for > half-filled.
